title: Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors & SVD
interviewAnswer: An eigenvector v of square A satisfies Av=λv, so its direction is preserved and scaled by eigenvalue λ. General matrices may have complex eigenvalues or lack a full eigenbasis; real symmetric matrices have orthonormal eigenvectors and real eigenvalues. Any m×n matrix has an SVD `A=UΣVᵀ`: V gives orthonormal input directions, Σ nonnegative gains, and U the corresponding output directions. Singular values expose rank and conditioning, and keeping the top k terms gives the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius and spectral norm. PCA is SVD/eigendecomposition applied to centered data/covariance, with preprocessing fitted on training data.
keyPoints: Truncation is optimal for reconstruction norms
PCA requires centering and leakage control
why: Decompositions power dimensionality reduction, compression, latent factors, spectral clustering, covariance analysis, stable least squares and condition diagnostics. Misuse is common: calling singular vectors eigenvectors, performing PCA without centering, fitting components before splitting, treating sign flips as model drift, or assuming high explained variance guarantees predictive value. First-principles geometry explains the outputs and their limitations.
intuition: A general matrix maps the unit sphere in its input space to an ellipsoid in its output space. Right singular vectors are orthogonal input directions along the ellipsoid's axes; singular values are their stretch factors; left singular vectors point along the resulting output axes. Eigenvectors instead ask for directions that remain on their own line inside the same square input/output space.
deepDive: The full explanation is organized into the structured sections below.
math: Eigenpair: Av=λv for square A and v≠0. SVD: A=UΣV^T with orthonormal U,V and σ_i≥0. Then A^TA v_i=σ_i²v_i and AA^T u_i=σ_i²u_i. Rank-r A has r positive singular values. The truncated A_k=Σ_{i=1}^kσ_i u_i v_i^T minimizes ||A−B||_2 and ||A−B||_F over rank(B)≤k, with ||A−A_k||_F²=Σ_{i>k}σ_i².
workedExample: Its eigenvectors and singular vectors are the coordinate axes. Eigenvalues are 3 and 1; singular values are also 3 and 1 because A is symmetric positive. Full SVD reconstructs A exactly. The best rank-one approximation keeps `3 e1 e1^T`, producing diag(3,0). Its spectral error is 1 and squared Frobenius error is 1, equal to the discarded singular value contributions. If the second axis contained crucial rare-class information, optimal reconstruction error would not guarantee optimal classification. A sign flip of e1 in both left/right vectors represents the same component.

commonMistakes.mistake: Every square matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis.
commonMistakes.correction: Real symmetric matrices do; general matrices may be non-normal, defective or have complex eigenpairs.

commonMistakes.mistake: PCA on all data before splitting is harmless preprocessing.
commonMistakes.correction: The mean and components learn validation/test distribution, causing leakage; fit only on training data.

commonMistakes.mistake: Component sign changes indicate a different solution.
commonMistakes.correction: Singular/eigenvectors are sign-ambiguous, and repeated/near-equal values permit basis rotations; compare subspaces/reconstruction.

followUps.question: How are eigenvalues and singular values related?
followUps.answer: Singular values of A are square roots of eigenvalues of positive-semidefinite A^TA; they are nonnegative and apply to rectangular A.

followUps.question: What does a tiny singular value imply?
followUps.answer: The map nearly erases that input direction, so inversion/coefficients can amplify noise and the problem is ill-conditioned.

followUps.question: What does truncated SVD optimize?
followUps.answer: Matrix reconstruction error among rank-k approximations under spectral and Frobenius norms, not every downstream objective.

production: Fit centering/scaling and decomposition on training data only; version representation, k, solver, seed and tolerances. Validate orthogonality, reconstruction, convergence, rank/condition and downstream metrics across slices. Use sparse/randomized operators for scale with exact-subset regression, control dtype/threads and monitor covariance/subspace drift. Protect sensitive components and roll back the transform with all dependent coordinates/models.
description: Eigenvectors identify directions preserved by a square linear transformation up to scale; singular value decomposition (SVD) gives an orthonormal input/output basis and nonnegative gains for any rectangular matrix. This chapter distinguishes eigendecomposition from SVD, derives their geometry, and connects them through `AᵀA` and `AAᵀ`. You will learn when a real matrix may lack a complete real eigenbasis, why symmetric matrices behave especially well, how singular values reveal rank and conditioning, and how truncated SVD yields the best low-rank approximation under standard norms. The chapter connects these ideas to principal component analysis, latent semantic structure, image compression, pseudoinverse and iterative power methods while separating centered covariance PCA from an uncentered matrix factorization. A worked 2×2 example verifies reconstruction and rank-one error. The lab implements power iteration and uses NumPy SVD with sign-invariant checks. Production guidance covers scaling, missing data, randomized algorithms, component stability, sign/rotation ambiguity, reconstruction versus downstream utility, privacy, resource cost and rollback. The aim is to make decompositions tools for understanding which directions a system amplifies, suppresses or cannot identify—not mysterious functions that merely return three arrays.
learningObjectives: Explain eigenvectors/eigenvalues and singular vectors/values geometrically and state when each decomposition applies.
Use singular values to reason about rank, conditioning, pseudoinverse, energy and optimal low-rank approximation.
Apply PCA or truncated SVD without leakage, centering mistakes or invalid interpretations of unstable components.

deepSections.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and symmetric structure
deepSections.body:
For square A, a nonzero vector v is an eigenvector if Av=λv. Scaling v gives the same direction, so normalization is conventional. Eigenvalues satisfy `det(A−λI)=0`. Repeated eigenvalues can have one or multiple independent eigenvectors. A matrix is diagonalizable when it has a basis of eigenvectors, giving `A=VΛV^{-1}` and making powers easy: `A^t=VΛ^tV^{-1}`. Not every matrix is diagonalizable, and real matrices can have complex eigenpairs.

Real symmetric matrices are special: the spectral theorem gives real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, `A=QΛQ^T`. Positive semidefinite matrices have nonnegative eigenvalues and define nonnegative quadratic forms. Covariance and Gram matrices have this structure, enabling stable geometric interpretation. For a Markov transition convention, a dominant eigenvector can describe stationary behavior under appropriate conditions; network spectral methods depend on which Laplacian/adjacency normalization is used.

Eigenvalue magnitude often governs repeated linear dynamics, but non-normal matrices can show transient amplification not predicted by eigenvalues alone. Eigenvector conditioning matters. Production conclusions should not reduce a general dynamical system to “largest eigenvalue wins” without checking diagonalizability, normalization and the actual operator.

deepSections.title: Singular value decomposition and fundamental subspaces
deepSections.body:
For A∈R^{m×n}, SVD is `A=UΣV^T`. In a reduced SVD of rank r, U has r orthonormal columns in R^m, V has r orthonormal columns in R^n, and diagonal Σ contains singular values `σ1≥…≥σr>0`. Applying A first expresses x in the right-singular basis V, scales components by σ, and expresses the result in U. Null-space right singular directions have zero gain.

The right singular vectors are eigenvectors of `A^TA` with eigenvalues σ²; left singular vectors are eigenvectors of `AA^T`. This connection avoids conflating dimensions: A's singular vectors live in different spaces when A is rectangular. Rank equals the number of nonzero singular values in exact arithmetic. The spectral norm is σ1, the Frobenius norm squared is the sum of σ_i², and full-rank condition number is σ1/σmin. Tiny values amplify noise in inverse problems.

The pseudoinverse `A^+=VΣ^+U^T` reverses nonzero directions and zeroes the null space. A tolerance determines which values count as numerical zero. Scaling features changes singular values, components and condition, so compare only under a fixed representation.

deepSections.title: Low-rank approximation and PCA
deepSections.body:
Writing SVD as `A=Σ_i σ_i u_i v_i^T` expresses A as rank-one components. The Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem says truncating after k components gives a best rank-k approximation under spectral and Frobenius norms. The squared Frobenius reconstruction error is `Σ_{i>k}σ_i²`. This is an optimal statement for those matrix norms, not necessarily for classification accuracy, fairness, interpretability or perceptual quality.

Principal component analysis centers data matrix X by the training mean. Right singular vectors of centered X are principal feature directions; scores are XV, and covariance eigenvalues are proportional to σ² depending on the covariance denominator. Explained variance ratio reports reconstruction variance, not supervised usefulness. Standardizing features changes PCA from covariance geometry toward correlation geometry and should follow unit/goal reasoning. Sparse/truncated SVD on term-document matrices is often applied without centering because centering destroys sparsity; call the method accurately.

Fit centering, scaling and components only on training data. Transform validation/test with those fitted parameters. Choose k using reconstruction, downstream validation, latency/storage and slice behavior. Component signs are arbitrary, and nearly equal singular values allow rotations within a subspace; compare subspaces or reconstructed outputs rather than raw columns alone.

deepSections.title: Algorithms and production operation
deepSections.body:
Dense full SVD is expensive for very large matrices. If only top components are needed, Lanczos/Krylov or randomized SVD methods use matrix-vector products and subspace iteration. Power iteration repeatedly normalizes Av to approach a dominant eigenvector when spectral separation and initialization conditions are favorable; convergence slows when leading magnitudes are close and can miss components orthogonal to initialization. Sparse and linear-operator interfaces avoid materializing huge matrices.

Validate reconstruction `A≈UΣV^T`, orthonormality `U^TU≈I`, `V^TV≈I`, sorted nonnegative values and expected residual. Use relative tolerances tied to dtype and norm. Compare randomized results across seeds by subspace angles or reconstruction, not signs. Monitor iteration convergence and fallback on nonconvergence. Mixed precision can distort small singular values, while oversubscribed BLAS threads can hurt latency.

Version row/feature definition, centering, scaling, missing-value treatment, k, solver, seed and tolerance. Monitor input scale/covariance drift, explained/reconstruction error, downstream metrics, component/subspace stability, latency and memory. Decompositions may encode sensitive population structure; restrict artifacts and evaluate subgroup effects. Keep a prior transform plus compatible downstream model/index for rollback, since changing the basis invalidates stored coordinates.

workedExamples.conclusion: Singular values quantify directional gain and reconstruction loss, but the downstream task decides whether a discarded direction matters.

exercises.prompt: Where do left and right singular vectors live for an m×n matrix?
exercises.solution: Left singular vectors live in the m-dimensional output space; right singular vectors live in the n-dimensional input space.

exercises.prompt: Why use truncated SVD for a sparse term-document matrix rather than centered PCA?
exercises.solution: Centering can destroy sparsity; uncentered truncated SVD preserves sparse computation, though its components are not covariance PCA.

exercises.prompt: Two runs have flipped component signs but identical reconstruction. Is that a failure?
exercises.solution: No. Signs are arbitrary when paired consistently. Compare reconstruction or subspace, not raw sign.

lab.goal: Implement dominant-eigenvector power iteration, then verify SVD reconstruction, orthogonality, sign-invariant eigen behavior and optimal rank-one error.
lab.buildIt:
import math

def power_iteration(a,start,steps=100):
    v=list(map(float,start))
    for _ in range(steps):
        w=[sum(row[j]*v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for row in a]
        norm=math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in w))
        if norm==0: raise ValueError('zero iterate')
        v=[x/norm for x in w]
    av=[sum(row[j]*v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for row in a]
    value=sum(v[i]*av[i] for i in range(len(v)))
    return value,v
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
A=np.array([[3.,0.],[0.,1.]])
value,vector=power_iteration(A.tolist(),[1.,1.])
U,s,Vt=np.linalg.svd(A,full_matrices=False)
rank1=s[0]*np.outer(U[:,0],Vt[0])
reconstruction=(U*s)@Vt
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(value-3.0)<1e-10
assert abs(abs(vector[0])-1.0)<1e-8
assert np.allclose(reconstruction,A)
assert np.allclose(U.T@U,np.eye(2)) and np.allclose(Vt@Vt.T,np.eye(2))
assert np.allclose(s,[3.,1.])
assert np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(A-rank1,2),s[1])
assert np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(A-rank1,'fro')**2,sum(s[1:]**2))
lab.shipIt: Use stable library/randomized decompositions, training-only preprocessing, convergence and reconstruction checks, versioned basis metadata, downstream slice evaluation, drift monitoring and compatible rollback artifacts.
